That is the inconsistency at the heart of this. I am not a climate denier and I will not be caricatured as one. I accept the science. I accept that we must reduce our emissions and that Ireland has obligations, both moral and legal, that we cannot wriggle out of. What I object to is a policy architecture that loads the cost onto the people least able to carry it while the structural drivers of the problem go untouched.

Consider the carbon tax. It is presented as a behavioural instrument, a price signal to change how people act. But a price signal only works where there is an alternative to switch to. In large parts of rural Ireland there is no bus, there is no train, there is no retrofit grant that covers the real cost of the work, and there is no prospect of any of those things arriving within the lifetime of this Government's targets. So the tax does not change behaviour. It simply extracts money from households that are already stretched, and it does so regressively, because fuel is a far larger share of a low income than a high one.

I want to see the ring-fenced revenue actually reaching those households. I want the retrofit schemes simplified so that an ordinary person can access them without hiring a consultant. And I want the Government to be honest with people about what is being asked of them, rather than dressing up revenue-raising measures as environmental leadership.

That is not tokenism. That is not a press release. That is steel in the ground and workers on the floor.

The member opposite would have Canadians believe that nothing is happening in this country, that our industrial base is withering and that the government is indifferent to it. I would gently invite him to visit the communities I have visited over the past year. I would invite him to speak to the workers at those plants, to the apprentices who are now entering the trades with confidence that there will be a job at the end of their training, and to the small suppliers in the surrounding region whose order books are full for the first time in a decade.

Does that mean everything is solved? Of course not. There are real pressures on the sector. Supply chains remain fragile. The cost of critical minerals is volatile, and we are competing against jurisdictions that are prepared to spend enormous sums to attract the same investment. I have never pretended otherwise, and members on this side have been candid about the scale of the challenge.

But there is a difference between acknowledging a challenge and running down one's own country. The member's speech was almost entirely the latter. He offered no plan of his own beyond the repeal of measures that are currently supporting the very workers he claims to speak for. If he has a serious alternative, let him bring it forward and we will debate it on the merits. What we will not accept is the suggestion that Canadian workers are being abandoned when the evidence in front of us says the opposite.

I have met the student representatives. I have read the submissions from the teacher unions, from the management bodies and from the parents' councils, and I have heard directly from young people who are frightened, who feel that their year has been stolen from them and who do not know what they are studying for. I do not dismiss any of that. It would be a very poor Minister who sat here and pretended that a postponement is a costless administrative adjustment. It is not. For a seventeen or eighteen year old, uncertainty of this kind is corrosive.

What I can say is this. We are working to a plan, and the plan involves running the examinations with the public health measures necessary to make them safe. That means smaller centres, more of them, additional invigilation, adjusted timetables and, where a student cannot sit an examination for reasons connected to the illness, a mechanism to ensure they are not penalised. Work is also being done on adjustments to the papers themselves to reflect the fact that teaching time has been lost and that the loss has not been evenly distributed across schools.

I want to be straight with the House. I cannot give an absolute guarantee about a date today, because that depends on the trajectory of the disease and on public health advice that I do not control. What I can guarantee is that no decision will be sprung on students without notice, that the sector will be consulted before any change is confirmed, and that whatever route we take, the qualification a student receives this year will carry the same standing as in any other year.

It could include support for local reconciliation committees, the kind of painstaking work where a faith leader sits down with elders on both sides of a dispute over grazing land or water access and finds an accommodation that no external agency could have brokered. It could include trauma counselling and psychosocial support for survivors of violence, which is very often delivered through churches, mosques and temples simply because they are the only functioning institutions left standing in a collapsed state.

It could also include early warning work. Faith networks frequently know that tensions are rising in a district weeks before that information reaches a capital city, let alone a donor government. Building channels so that information can travel quickly, and so that it is acted on, is itself peacebuilding, and it is extraordinarily cost-effective compared with the alternative of responding after violence has occurred.

I would add one caution, because the House would expect me to be honest about it. Faith-based organisations are not automatically forces for peace. In some contexts religious identity has been the very fault line along which violence has run, and there are actors who use the language of faith to mobilise hatred. Our approach therefore has to be discerning. We fund on the basis of demonstrated commitment to inclusive peacebuilding, with the same due diligence and the same safeguarding standards we would apply to any other partner.

But with that caveat firmly stated, I believe we have historically under-used these partnerships. The reach, the legitimacy and the sheer staying power of faith communities in fragile settings is an asset that a development programme ignores at its cost. My Department is looking closely at how our programming can better reflect that, and I would be glad to discuss the detail further with my hon. Friend.

I raise it not to mock the individual concerned, because there is often distress and sometimes genuine mental ill health behind claims of this kind, and I have no wish to add to anybody's difficulties. I raise it because of what happened next.

What happened next was that this claim, which perhaps thirty years ago would have circulated among a handful of people and gone no further, was amplified across social media platforms to an audience of hundreds of thousands. It was picked up, elaborated, monetised through advertising and subscription appeals, and woven into a broader set of narratives about the illegitimacy of our institutions. People sent money. People turned up at courts and at council offices asserting that the ordinary law did not apply to them because they had been persuaded that the entire constitutional order was a fraud.

That is the point I want the House to hold onto. The specific claim is absurd. The mechanism by which it spread is not absurd at all, and the same mechanism carries far more dangerous material. The platforms have no meaningful incentive to intervene, because engagement of this kind is precisely what their systems are designed to promote. Outrage and revelation perform well. Careful correction does not.

So when Ministers tell us that the existing framework is adequate, I would ask them to look at cases like this one and ask whether it really is. I am not arguing for the state to become an arbiter of historical truth; that would be a cure worse than the disease. I am arguing that where a platform's own algorithmic choices actively promote demonstrably false and harmful material to people who are vulnerable to it, that is a design decision, and design decisions can be regulated.

A nation-to-nation relationship means that the other nation is at the table when the text is drafted, not consulted after the fact on a document that is already substantially settled. It means that when rights holders say a provision does not work, the provision changes. It means that consent is a real thing with a real possibility of being withheld, because a consent that can only ever be granted is not consent at all.

I want to be fair. There are provisions in this bill that communities in my riding have asked for and that will make a practical difference. I am not going to stand here and pretend otherwise for the sake of a partisan point. But I have also sat with leadership who told me they learned the contents of the bill from a news release, and I have read submissions from nations who set out specific, drafted amendments and received no substantive response. When that is the pattern, the language of partnership starts to wear thin, and people notice.

The risk is not simply that a particular bill is imperfect. The risk is that the word itself gets used up. If reconciliation becomes a term that governments deploy to describe whatever they were going to do anyway, then in ten years it will carry no weight at all, and we will need a new word, and the underlying work will still be undone.

So I will support this bill going to committee, because I think it can be improved there and because the communities I represent need the parts of it that work. But I would ask the government to treat the committee stage as a genuine opportunity to hear amendments, rather than as an obstacle to be managed.

Let me take the police first, because Ministers keep reaching for a headline figure of new recruits without acknowledging what that figure actually represents. It represents, at best, the partial replacement of officers who were cut over the preceding decade. It does not restore the experience that walked out of the door with them. A newly attested constable is not equivalent to a sergeant with fifteen years on a neighbourhood team who knows every family on the estate and can head off trouble with a conversation. We lost that knowledge, and it is not recoverable through a recruitment campaign.

On local government, the position is worse. Councils in my region have absorbed reductions in central funding of a scale that no private organisation could have survived, and they have done it while their statutory duties, particularly in adult social care and children's services, have grown relentlessly. The result is not a leaner council. The result is a council that spends almost everything it has on two statutory services and has effectively ceased to do anything else. Everything discretionary has gone. That is why the high street looks the way it does.

And the Bill in front of us does nothing about any of it. It contains reliefs that will be enjoyed overwhelmingly by those already comfortable, funded by a freeze in thresholds that drags ordinary earners into higher rates without a single Minister having to stand up and announce a tax rise. That is not fairness. It is a tax rise by stealth, presented as a tax cut, and the public are considerably less easily fooled than the Chancellor appears to believe.

That is the heart of my objection. It is not that discretion exists within the correctional system. Discretion has to exist; no set of rules can anticipate every circumstance, and I would not want to legislate away the professional judgment of people who actually know the offender in front of them. My objection is to the absence of any duty to inform, to consult or to justify.

A victim's family should not learn from a journalist that the person who killed their child has been moved to a facility with unfenced grounds and access to community programming. They should be told in advance, by someone whose job it is to tell them, and they should have a route to make representations before the decision takes effect. That is not a radical proposition. It does not require us to override professional assessment. It requires us to treat the people most affected by these decisions as participants rather than as an afterthought.

The government's response so far has been to say that the relevant policies were reviewed and that directives have been issued. I have read those directives. They restate existing practice in slightly firmer language, and they impose no enforceable obligation on anyone. When the next case arises, and there will be a next case, the family will be in exactly the position this family was in.

We can fix that in this bill. Amendments have been tabled that would do it. I would urge members opposite to look at them on their merits rather than on the basis of who tabled them.

We are told repeatedly that this is a decade of delivery, that the technology is proven, that the investment community is ready and that the only remaining question is one of sequencing. And yet the project I am describing has now been through three separate rounds of feasibility assessment, each of which has broadly confirmed the conclusions of the one before it, and we are no closer to a spade in the ground than we were when I first raised this in the House.

The consequence of that delay is not neutral. Skilled people do not sit and wait. The engineering firms in my constituency that built up capability in anticipation of this work have, in several cases, redeployed those teams to projects overseas, and once that capability is dispersed it is slow and expensive to rebuild. The supply chain follows the certainty, and at the moment the certainty is elsewhere.

There is also a question of trust. Communities in south Wales have heard promises about transformative investment before. They have heard about enterprise zones, about growth deals, about clusters and corridors and hubs. In many cases what actually arrived was a fraction of what was announced, arriving years later, and delivering a fraction of the jobs. People are not cynical because they are ungenerous. They are cynical because they have been paying attention.

So my ask of the Minister is specific rather than rhetorical. Will she set out a date by which the funding decision will be taken? Will she confirm which department holds the decision, because that has been genuinely unclear? many parts of the country the local authority has become little more than a delivery agent for central government schemes, administering programmes it did not design, to criteria it cannot vary, with funding it cannot plan around because it arrives in annual tranches with conditions attached. That is not local government. That is local administration, and the two are not the same thing.

When I was first elected to a council, the authority ran its own housing programme. It built houses, it maintained them, it allocated them, and if a tenant had a problem there was a named person in a building on the main street who was accountable for fixing it. Over successive decades that capacity was dismantled, first through the transfer of functions to national agencies and then through the simple attrition of not replacing the staff who left. We now have a situation where councils are expected to deliver ambitious housing targets while possessing a fraction of the technical staff, the architects, the quantity surveyors and the clerks of works, that they had a generation ago.

So I welcome the provisions in this Bill that begin to restore some of that, but I want to press the Minister on two points. First, functions without resources are a trap. If we hand back responsibility without the staff and the multi-annual funding to exercise it, we set councils up to fail and then use the failure as evidence that the centre should have kept control. Second, we need to look seriously at the balance between the executive and the elected members. Councillors in this country have less real power than their counterparts almost anywhere in western Europe, and people notice that the person they vote for cannot actually change very much.

If we are serious about local democracy, those two things have to be addressed together. I look forward to the Minister's response on both.

On the substantive point that lies behind the hon. Member's question, I think there is a legitimate debate to be had about the resilience of the systems we now depend on. We have, over recent years, introduced a good deal of technology into the operation of the House, some of it very successfully. Members can now do things remotely that would have been unthinkable a decade ago, and the institution is more accessible to Members with caring responsibilities and to those with disabilities than it was. That is a real gain and I would not want to lose it.

But every one of those systems is a dependency, and dependencies fail. What matters is whether there is a fallback that works, that everybody understands, and that can be invoked without a lengthy discussion about whether it is in order. In this case there was, and it functioned, albeit slowly.

What I would say to the House authorities, and I will say it to them directly rather than only across the Dispatch Box, is that the fallback arrangements ought to be rehearsed rather than merely documented. It is one thing to have a procedure written down; it is another for the people who have to operate it at nine o'clock at night to have practised it.

We have reflected carefully on that feedback and I can confirm to the House that we have brought forward amendments in response.

The concern raised, in essence, was that the original drafting gave the appointing bodies a power of removal expressed in fairly broad terms, without a clear procedural framework around its exercise. The Institution's view, which I think is a reasonable one, was that arbitrators need to be confident in the security of their position if they are to make robust determinations, some of which will inevitably be unwelcome to one party or the other. An arbitrator who is looking over their shoulder is not an independent arbitrator, and the whole scheme depends on independence being real and being seen to be real.

The amendments therefore do three things. First, they specify the grounds on which removal may be sought, rather than leaving them to be inferred. Second, they require that the arbitrator be given notice and an opportunity to make representations before any decision is taken. Third, they provide for the appointing body to record its reasons in writing, which will bring the process within the ordinary reach of judicial review should that ever prove necessary.

I should say that we have not accepted every suggestion that was put to us. There was a proposal for a full appellate mechanism, and we concluded that this would be disproportionate. The volume of cases these bodies will handle is significant, the timescales are deliberately compressed, and building in a further tier of challenge would risk defeating the object of the scheme, which is to resolve disputes quickly and at low cost. We think the safeguards we have introduced strike the right balance.

I am grateful to the Royal Institution for engaging so constructively, and to Members in the other place who pressed the point. I commend the amendments to the House.

It is elementary. And yet the reason this provision is in front of us is that in a series of well-documented cases over the past two decades, it was not possible to do it at all.

Women who received defective implants could not be traced because the records were held in paper form by private clinics, some of which had since ceased trading. Patients with faulty hip replacements were identified over a period of years rather than weeks, and some were never identified. The cost of that failure is measured in avoidable revision surgery, in chronic pain and, in some cases, in deaths that a functioning registry would have prevented.

Subsection (5) is therefore not administrative housekeeping. It is the operative provision that determines whether the system we are creating will actually work when it is needed. That is why I have tabled the amendments the Committee will come to shortly, which seek to ensure that the categories of information specified are sufficient for the purpose. In particular, a device identifier without a reliable link to the patient record is of very limited use, and a patient record without the identity of the implanting clinician makes it far harder to detect a cluster arising from a particular technique rather than a particular product.

I recognise the sensitivity here, and I want to address it directly rather than have it raised against me. This is health data of the most personal kind, and any system holding it must be built with strict access controls, clear purposes and effective sanction for misuse. I do not accept, though, that privacy and safety are in genuine tension in this instance. The patients who were failed were failed precisely because their data was nowhere at all.

If that is what he meant, it would be a significant and welcome development, and I want it on the record. If it is not what he meant, I want to know that too, because the cities concerned have been strung along on this question for the better part of a decade.

Limerick has had its plebiscite. The people of Limerick voted for a directly elected mayor. That was not a consultation exercise or an opinion survey; it was a vote, and it produced a result, and the State's response to that result has been a series of implementation reports, working groups and legislative timetables that have slipped repeatedly. Meanwhile Cork and Waterford voted the other way, in circumstances where, I would argue, nobody could tell the electorate what powers the office would actually hold, and Galway was never asked at all.

That is not a coherent way to reform local government. It is reform by attrition, and it produces the worst of all outcomes, which is a public that concludes the whole exercise is not serious.

So my questions to the Taoiseach are these. First, will the legislation providing for the Limerick office be enacted this session, and will the office be filled at the next local elections rather than at some unspecified later date? Second, what functions will actually transfer to that office, because a mayor with a title and no powers will discredit the model rather than demonstrate it? Third, does the Government intend to return to Cork, Waterford and Galway with a concrete proposition, and on what timescale?

I ask these in a constructive spirit. I support the principle. But I have watched this file for long enough to know that principle without a date is not a commitment.

They are the words of a leader who regards the independence of those neighbours as a historical error awaiting correction, and we should have the honesty to say so plainly rather than continuing to search for a form of words that will not give offence.

For twenty years, a great deal of Western policy has been constructed on the assumption that this was rhetoric, that it was a matter of domestic positioning, and that the underlying relationship remained transactional and therefore manageable. We built pipelines on that assumption. We admitted capital into our financial system on that assumption. We allowed a substantial part of our energy supply to depend on it, and we told ourselves that interdependence would produce restraint.

It did not produce restraint. It produced leverage, and the leverage ran in one direction, because a state prepared to accept economic pain for strategic ends will always have the advantage over states that are not.

I do not say this to score points against those who took those decisions. Many of them were taken in good faith and with cross-party support, mine included in some instances. But we are now in a position where we have to unwind them at speed and at cost, and we should be candid with the public about what that will mean, because the bill will land on households and businesses before it lands anywhere else.

What I would ask of the Government is that the response be structural rather than episodic. Sanctions matter, but sanctions announced in response to each new outrage and then quietly eroded are worse than useless. We need an approach that assumes this behaviour will continue, because on the evidence of the past two decades, it will.

The scale of this is not marginal. We are talking about very large numbers of people who have no entitlement to sick pay, no holiday pay, no protection against unfair dismissal and no pension contribution from the organisation whose work they are doing, often to a schedule that organisation sets, using equipment that organisation supplies, wearing a uniform with that organisation's name on it. The legal fiction that such a person is running their own business in an open market is precisely that, a fiction, and it is a fiction that the courts have repeatedly been obliged to unpick case by case, at great expense, because the statutory framework is so unclear.

That case-by-case approach places the entire burden on the worker. To establish their status they must bring a claim, usually without representation, usually against a well-resourced opponent, and usually while no longer being offered work. The predictable result is that most do not bring a claim at all, and the practice continues.

What we propose is straightforward in principle. A single clear statutory test, with a presumption of employment where the indicators point that way, and the burden placed on the engager to demonstrate otherwise. Alignment, over time, between employment law status and tax status, so that the incentive to misclassify is removed at source rather than policed after the fact. And an enforcement body with the resources to act on patterns rather than waiting for individuals to complain.

But let me go further, because I do not think the member's argument fails only on the numbers. It fails on the diagnosis. The pressures facing young Canadians today are not primarily about the absence of a program. They are about the cost of housing, and about the fact that a generation is looking at the price of a home in the city where they grew up and concluding that the arithmetic simply does not work for them. I hear that in every conversation I have with people under thirty-five, and I do not dismiss it, because they are right.

That is a supply problem that has been building for thirty years, under governments of both stripes, driven by municipal zoning, by the collapse of purpose-built rental construction, by the loss of skilled trades capacity and by an approach to land use that treated housing as an asset class first and a place to live second. It will not be solved by a slogan, and it will not be solved in one budget.

What this government has done is put federal money on the table conditional on municipalities actually changing the rules that block construction, which is the lever that matters. Members opposite voted against that. They are entitled to do so, but they cannot then come to this chamber and lament the plight of young people without accounting for the vote.

I would welcome a serious debate about whether the conditions attached are the right ones, whether the disbursement is fast enough, and whether the targets are ambitious enough. Those are legitimate questions and I have some of my own. What I will not accept is the premise that nothing is being done.

I understand the concern in the community, and the Deputy has articulated it well on a number of occasions. This is not simply a building. It is a site in the centre of a rapidly growing town, with a hall, playing fields and accommodation that community organisations have used for decades, in many cases informally and without any written arrangement. I want to be clear about the position. Where a property is surplus to the requirements of the education sector, the first consideration is whether it is required by another part of the education system, including for a special school, an additional primary provision or a further education facility. My Department is examining that question now in light of the demographic projections for the area, and Maynooth's projections are, as the Deputy knows, exceptionally strong.

If the property is not required for educational purposes, the next stage involves engagement with other State bodies and with the local authority, which may have a use for it in the context of its own service provision or its development plan. Disposal on the open market is the last option, not the first.

I would encourage the local authority and the community groups concerned to make their case formally and in writing to KWETB at this stage, because a documented proposition is considerably easier to act upon than a general expression of interest. I am happy to facilitate a meeting if that would help.

I want to acknowledge that some of the underlying constraints are genuine and are not the invention of any Minister. There is a shortage of skilled labour in the construction sector, the result of a decade in which we told a generation of apprentices that there was no future in the trade and watched them emigrate. There is a materials cost problem driven by international factors. There is a financing environment that has turned sharply against apartment development in particular. None of that is fixed by good intentions in this Chamber.

But the State has levers it is not pulling. It owns land, a great deal of it, some of it serviced and zoned and sitting idle while we debate. It owns a housing agency and it owns local authorities with a historical record of direct delivery at scale that we appear to have collectively forgotten. Between 1948 and the mid-1970s local authorities in this country built housing in volumes that would be regarded as fantastical today, and they did it without the private sector's cost of capital and without a developer's margin.

So when I say we must step up, I mean specifically that the State must return to being a builder rather than a subsidiser of other people's building. Every scheme that operates by improving a purchaser's ability to bid in a supply-constrained market pushes the price up. That is not ideology; it is arithmetic, and the ESRI has said so.

I would ask the Minister to set out, in this year's plan, the number of units the local authorities themselves will construct, distinct from acquisitions, leases and Part V. That is the number that will tell us whether trust is warranted.

That, I think, is the crux of the matter for the great majority of my constituents, and it is worth stating plainly rather than allowing the debate to disappear into technical vocabulary that most people quite reasonably find impenetrable.

The objection is not to a backstop as such. Nobody I have spoken to wants to see infrastructure at the border in Ireland, and nobody wishes to unpick an agreement that ended a conflict. The objection is to an arrangement that binds one party indefinitely at the discretion of the other. In any commercial negotiation, an agreement that you cannot leave without the counterparty's permission is not an agreement between equals, and every Member of this House knows that.

What the compromise offers is a route through. It accepts the obligation not to create a hard border. It proposes to meet that obligation through alternative arrangements, trusted trader schemes, technology-assisted declarations, exemptions for small traders, all of which exist in some form at other borders in the world. The principle at the heart of this legislation is a simple one, and I think it commands broad support in this House whatever differences we may have on the detail. It is that the State should not, through its investment arm, be a financial participant in activity that our own foreign policy declares to be illegal. There is an incoherence in maintaining a diplomatic position at the United Nations while our sovereign fund holds equity in the companies whose operations give that position its subject matter. Whatever one's view of the underlying conflict, that incoherence is not defensible.

I have heard the arguments against. The first is that divestment is symbolic and will change nothing on the ground. That may be true of any single fund's decision, but the argument proves too much, since it would apply equally to every sanction and every boycott ever imposed, including ones that this House has supported and that history has vindicated. The second argument is that a fiduciary duty prevents it. I do not accept that a fiduciary duty compels a public fund to hold assets its owner has determined to be inconsistent with public policy, and the legislation resolves any doubt.

The third argument is the one I take most seriously, which is the question of where the line is drawn and whether a precedent set here will be demanded elsewhere on less clear facts. That is a genuine difficulty and I do not have a complete answer to it. My view is that the illegality here has been determined by bodies whose authority we accept, which gives us a workable criterion rather than a purely political one.

I support the Bill and I hope the Government will not obstruct it.

legislation before us today reflects a considered approach to bail reform that balances the presumption of innocence, which is constitutionally protected and which no member of this House should treat lightly, against the legitimate expectation of Canadians that a person who poses a demonstrable risk of serious harm will not be released to reoffend.

That balance is difficult and I want to acknowledge the difficulty rather than pretending it away. Detention before trial is detention of a person who has not been convicted of anything. Every day of it is a day taken from someone who may ultimately be acquitted, and the evidence shows that those days fall disproportionately on Indigenous people, on Black Canadians and on people with mental illness and addiction. A reform that simply detains more people will worsen an injustice that the courts have repeatedly told us is already severe.

So what does this bill actually do? It creates a reverse onus in a defined and narrow set of circumstances, principally repeat violent offending with a weapon, where the empirical case for it is strongest. It does not create a general presumption against release. It does not alter the ladder principle. And it is accompanied by investment in supervision and in bail support programs, because the alternative to detention is not release with nothing, it is release with conditions that are actually monitored, and at present in most of this country they are not.

The member opposite would go considerably further and would, if I understand his party's position, apply a reverse onus to a much wider category. I would put this to him. That is not a safer community. That is a system failing in a different direction.

What we have done, with the best of intentions and for reasons that were entirely sound at the outset, is to protect people from a virus by removing from them the thing that gives their remaining life its content. On the Deputy's substantive point, which concerns whether the campaign should be broadened, I have some sympathy but I would enter two notes of caution.

The first is that a general campaign advocating vaccination in the abstract tends to be considerably less effective than a specific campaign about a specific vaccine delivered through a trusted individual, which in practice usually means the general practitioner or the public health nurse. The evidence on this is quite consistent. Broad awareness campaigns shift attitudes marginally; a conversation with a clinician shifts behaviour.

The second is that a campaign framed as a response to misinformation can inadvertently amplify the misinformation, by introducing the claim to people who had not previously encountered it and by framing the issue as contested when it is not. Communications research is fairly clear on this and it is a genuine constraint on what can usefully be done from the centre.

What I think is more promising, and what we are pursuing, is investment in the delivery infrastructure. Where uptake is low, it is very often not because parents refuse but because the appointment was inconvenient, the school programme visited on a day the child was absent, or nobody followed up. Catch-up clinics and active follow-up produce larger gains, per euro, than advertising.

Now, the hon. Member asks whether this House will legislate in the absence of an Executive.
